content: Teenage pregnancy is defined in the United States as a girl under the age of majority becoming pregnant. In the United Kingdom, a woman is considered a pregnant teenager if she becomes pregnant before her 18th birthday. The term generally refers to pregnancies in individuals who have not yet reached legal adulthood, which varies globally. The average age of menarche (the first menstrual period) in the United States is 12.5 years, though this varies by ethnicity and weight. Ovulation may occur irregularly after menarche. The average age of menarche has been declining over time. Whether fertility leads to early pregnancy depends on a combination of societal and personal factors. Globally, teenage pregnancy rates range from 143 per 1,000 in sub-Saharan Africa to 2.9 per 1,000 in South Korea. Pregnant teenagers face many of the same obstetric challenges as women in their 20s and 30s. However, younger mothers, particularly those under 15 and those in developing countries, face additional medical risks. For mothers aged 15 to 19, age itself is not a direct risk factor, but socioeconomic factors may contribute to additional risks. Data from developed countries show that teenage pregnancy is associated with lower educational attainment, higher poverty rates, and poorer life outcomes for the children of teenage mothers. Teenage pregnancies in developed countries are often outside of marriage and carry significant social stigma in many communities and cultures. In developing countries, teenage pregnancies are more likely to occur within marriage and are less stigmatized. Annually, 13 million children are born to women under 20 worldwide, with over 90% of these births occurring in developing countries. Complications from pregnancy and childbirth are the leading cause of mortality among women aged 15 to 19 in these regions. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest teenage pregnancy rates globally, often linked to early marriage. For example, in Niger, 87% of women surveyed were married, and 53% had given birth before the age of 18. In South Africa, the introduction of child support grants in 1999 has been linked to an increase in teenage pregnancies. In the Indian subcontinent, early marriage often leads to adolescent pregnancies, particularly in rural areas where rates are higher than in urbanized regions. However, rates of early marriage and pregnancy have decreased significantly in countries like Indonesia and Malaysia, though they remain relatively high. Industrialized Asian nations such as South Korea and Singapore have some of the lowest teenage birth rates globally. In Europe, since the 1970s, there has been a trend of decreasing total fertility rates, an increase in the age of first childbirth, and a decline in teenage births. The United Kingdom has the highest teenage birth rate in Europe and a higher abortion rate than most European countries. In contrast, many Western European countries have very low teenage pregnancy rates, attributed to comprehensive sex education, high contraceptive use, traditional values, or a combination of these factors. In the United States, teenage birth rates are the highest among developed nations, and teenage abortion rates are also high. However, teenage pregnancy rates have been declining significantly since the early 1990s across all racial groups. African-American and Hispanic teenagers still have higher rates compared to European-American and Asian-American teenagers. The Guttmacher Institute attributes 25% of the decline to abstinence and 75% to effective contraceptive use. In Canada, teenage birth rates have also steadily declined. Factors contributing to teenage pregnancy include early marriage, traditional gender roles, lack of contraceptive use, and societal norms. In some societies, early pregnancy is seen as a sign of fertility. In developed countries, most teenage pregnancies are unplanned. Alcohol and drug use may also reduce inhibitions, leading to unintended sexual activity. Age discrepancies in relationships are a significant factor in teenage pregnancies. Teenage girls with older partners, particularly adult men, are more likely to become pregnant and carry the pregnancy to term. Studies have shown that a majority of births to teenage girls in the United States are fathered by adult men aged 20 or older. Sexual abuse is another contributing factor, with a significant proportion of teenage pregnancies resulting from rape or unwanted sexual experiences. Socioeconomic factors such as poverty are strongly associated with teenage pregnancy. Economically disadvantaged countries have higher rates of teenage mothers compared to wealthier nations. In the UK, teenage pregnancies are concentrated in the most deprived populations. Childhood environments characterized by abuse, domestic violence, and family strife increase the likelihood of teenage pregnancy. Girls raised in foster care or without a father present are at higher risk. Efforts to reduce teenage pregnancies include comprehensive sex education, improved access to contraception, and support for teenage mothers. In the UK, the Teenage Pregnancy Strategy aims to reduce teenage pregnancies and improve social inclusion for teenage mothers and their families. In the United States, sex education remains a contentious issue, with some schools promoting abstinence-only programs and others offering comprehensive education. The Dutch approach, which emphasizes values, communication skills, and access to healthcare, is often seen as a model. Medical outcomes for teenage mothers and their children are concerning. Pregnant teenagers are less likely to receive adequate prenatal care, leading to higher rates of premature birth and low birth weight. Nutritional deficiencies and lack of access to high-quality medical care exacerbate these issues. In developing countries, complications from pregnancy and childbirth result in the deaths of an estimated 70,000 teenage girls annually. Young mothers and their babies are also at greater risk of contracting HIV.
